extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners of social/political persuasion and crowd psychology (e.g., political actors, propagandists, mass-communication strategists)
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and factors governing how crowds form beliefs and can be influenced; descriptive rules about what kinds of stimuli and forms of presentation succeed in moving crowds and what deep social factors prepare them to accept ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crowds do not reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowds do not reason; they accept or reject ideas as a whole, tolerate neither discussion nor contradiction, and suggestions invade their entire understanding and tend at once to transform themselves into acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt to persuade crowds by logical demonstration or detailed argument; appeals to intelligence are ineffective. Use non-rational, immediate means (example: Antony's reading of Caesar's will succeeded where rhetoric would not).

rubrics_metrics.name: Impress the imagination with a startling, very clear image
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever strikes the imagination of crowds presents itself under the shape of a startling and very clear image, freed from all accessory explanation, or merely having as accompaniment a few marvellous or mysterious facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Condense events into a single vivid image (victory, miracle, great crime, great hope). Keep explanations minimal; favour spectacle and simple, memorable images over complex narratives or caveats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present things as a whole; do not indicate genesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Things must be laid before the crowd as a whole, and their genesis must never be indicated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid causal histories, nuanced origins, or stepwise explanations. Give the crowd a simple, self-contained picture or story rather than a chain of causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: One great visible event outweighs many small facts
rubrics_metrics.description: A single great crime or a single great accident will profoundly impress the crowd, whereas a hundred petty crimes or petty accidents will not strike the imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritise dramatizing singular, spectacular incidents rather than presenting many small statistics or dispersed facts. Emphasize the singular, memorable instance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visible images beat statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not the facts in themselves that strike the popular imagination, but the way in which they are brought under notice; an epidemic given as weekly statistics made little impression, whereas a dramatic visible accident would.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid reliance on statistical evidence when trying to mobilize public feeling; convert abstract numbers into striking, visible, humanized images or scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid persuasion by demonstration; use immediate emotional triggers
rubrics_metrics.description: The feat of impressing the imagination of crowds is never achieved by attempting to work upon the intelligence or reasoning faculty, that is to say, by way of demonstration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use immediate emotional triggers—spectacle, symbolic acts, dramatic gestures, or revealed artifacts—rather than logical chains of proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convictions of crowds assume a religious shape
rubrics_metrics.description: When examined, convictions of crowds always assume the peculiar form of a religious sentiment: worship of a supposed superior being, fear of its power, blind submission to its commands, inability to discuss its dogmas, desire to spread them, and tendency to consider as enemies all who do not accept them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To secure uncritical adherence, present ideas in a quasi-religious form: create a supreme object (leader/idea), rituals or symbols, and frame dissent as hostile. This obviates discussion and solidifies adherence (historical examples: Reformation, Revolution, cults of leaders).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use symbolic iconography (portraits, statues) to foster worship
rubrics_metrics.description: Great men no longer have altars but have statues or portraits in the hands of their admirers, and the cult accorded them is not notably different from religious worship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deploy visual symbols—portraits, statues, badges, ceremonies—that function like altars to focus reverence and strengthen emotional bonds to the leader or cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit the crowd's tendency from sympathy to adoration and antipathy to hatred
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowds only entertain violent and extreme sentiments; sympathy quickly becomes adoration, and antipathy is almost as soon as aroused transformed into hatred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design messages to convert sympathy into adoration and to identify or demonize opponents to convert antipathy into sustained hostility; be aware this also risks promoting intolerance and fanaticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remote factors shape what ideas can take hold (race)
rubrics_metrics.description: Race (national/ethnic character) exerts predominating influence: it represents the suggestions of ancestors and determines which ideas a people can easily accept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor appeals to the inherited character and predispositions of a population; expect different crowds in different countries to respond to distinct stimuli. One-size-fits-all messages will fail across racial/cultural contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remote factors shape beliefs (traditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditions are the synthesis of the soul of the race, weigh with immense force, and crowds cling tenaciously to traditional ideas; changes usually affect names and outward forms only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect and work within longstanding traditions; radical reforms that ignore tradition will be resisted or only alter surface forms. Effective influence often requires gradual change aligned with tradition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remote factors shape beliefs (time)
rubrics_metrics.description: Time prepares the opinions and beliefs of crowds: it is the sole real creator and destroyer, accumulating the past that allows certain ideas to germinate at given epochs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that some ideas need long preparatory periods; patience and timing matter—attempts to force premature changes are likely to fail. Use historical sequencing to create receptive conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remote factors shape beliefs (institutions are effects, not causes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Political and social institutions are the product of race and customs, not the creators of them; institutions have no intrinsic virtue and cannot by themselves transform a people's character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume reforming institutions alone will change popular beliefs; messaging should address underlying cultural character and not rely solely on legal or institutional prescriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remote factors shape beliefs (instruction and education have limited and varied effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction is widely thought to improve men, but psychology and experience show it need not make men more moral; certain types of education (e.g., rote Latin systems) can be demoralising and even correlate with increases in criminality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be skeptical that education alone will shift crowd convictions. Consider the content and method of education in your audience analysis; poorly directed instruction can backfire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immediate factors produce sudden action on prepared soil
rubrics_metrics.description: Immediate factors (speeches, orators, visible incidents) coming on top of long preparatory work cause ideas to take shape and lead crowds to sudden resolutions—riots, strikes, or the election of a leader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine long-term groundwork (remote factors) with well-timed immediate stimuli (powerful speeches, spectacles, or incidents) to trigger mass action. Timing and delivery are decisive.
